item.title: Brazilian scientists sampled 800 trees across 63 Amazon locations; their atomic fingerprinting...
item.description: Brazilian scientists are innovating with an isotopic mapping model designed to tackle illegal logging head-on. This novel forensic tool examines atomic signatures within trees, allowing them to trace the origination of timber effectively. Currently, the model can eliminate ninety-two percent of the Amazon rainforest from potential illegal wood sources, utilizing stable isotope analysis for secure chemical fingerprinting. The goal is to bolster law enforcement investigations and diminish global timber crime.

item.title: Researchers mapped 128 million US buildings for landslide exposure; 6.5 million Americans live in...
item.description: A recent study identifies millions of Americans at risk from landslide hazards, revealing that densely populated eastern states have higher exposure. The challenges mount for rural communities when recovery from landslides is needed, contrasting with wealthier cities that implement zoning and engineering strategies to minimize risk. The findings stress the importance of increased public investment and disaster aid for rural areas facing these dangers.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Virginia students save family from lake during golf tryouts
item.description: Three Culpeper teenagers are heroes after rescuing a family whose kayaks overturned. They heard a splash and a child screaming, then immediately acted. The teens swam to the struggling family and brought them safely back to shore. Police and school officials praised their quick thinking and courage. Their actions highlight the importance of immediate response in water emergencies.

item.title: In 1925, the world’s first motel opened in California with rooms for $1.25; after closing in 1991...
item.description: The iconic site of the world's first motel in San Luis Obispo is now on the market. With various redevelopment options available, buyers are encouraged to re-envision this historic property. Established in 1925 and ceasing operations in 1991, this site presents a unique opportunity to either preserve or transform a piece of hospitality history amidst the recent trend of revitalizing classic motels into boutique experiences.

item.title: 9,000 discarded Christmas trees help restore New Orleans wetlands
item.description: New Orleans is giving used Christmas trees a second life by dropping them into coastal marshes to help slow land loss. The bundled trees trap sediment, reduce wave energy and support marsh grass growth. Scientists say the method helps restore wetlands in selected areas but is only one part of Louisiana's broader coastal protection efforts.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: You can make yourselves ‘luckier’: Science-backed tips to rewire your brain for luck
item.description: Cultivating a belief in your own luck can reshape your brain to recognize new opportunities. By documenting moments of serendipity, you start to see that luck is more frequent than originally believed. Individuals branded as unlucky often experience heightened anxiety, which narrows their perspective. In contrast, self-proclaimed lucky individuals expect good things and interact more openly. Ultimately, creating your own luck demands conscious choices and more frequent attempts.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Bordeaux vineyards escaped the immediate wildfires, but repeated heatwaves are shrinking...
item.description: European vineyards face an early harvest due to prolonged heat and drought conditions. Wildfires across southwestern France and Greece have forced thousands to evacuate their homes. Emergency services continue to battle numerous blazes, particularly in Greece and on Crete. Spain sees some relief as national emergency declarations are lifted in certain areas. Record continent-wide warmth exacerbates fire risks and impacts air quality for millions.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Engineers linked two deep wells through 629°F rock beneath Oregon’s Newberry volcano; the experiment could unlock round-the-clock power without burning fuel
item.description: Mazama Energy connected two deep wells reaching 629 degrees Fahrenheit. This marks the world's hottest enhanced geothermal system ever built. The company plans three more wells in 2026 targeting hotter rock. This project aims to unlock superhot rock for cleaner energy production. Geothermal energy could become a significant player in the clean energy mix.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: College students in US are choosing to live in retirement communities for affordable housing
item.description: College students in the US are moving into retirement communities, paying lower rent in exchange for volunteering with older residents. Supporters say the arrangement helps students find affordable housing while reducing loneliness for both generations and building meaningful relationships.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Teen's routine fishing trip ends with a South Dakota record that had stood since 1970
item.description: A routine fishing trip on South Dakota's Wall Lake turned into a record-breaking moment for teenager Jack Backman after he caught a one-pound pumpkinseed, setting a new state record. Thinking he had hooked a crappie, Backman was surprised to discover the rare catch. The fish beat a 12-ounce state record that had stood since 1970.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: How being poor damages your brain, new study finds
item.description: Long-term financial strain can significantly speed up the aging of the brain. Research highlights that persistent monetary worries contribute to cognitive decline, particularly noticeable by the age of fifty-three. Brain scans portray more severe shrinkage in individuals facing such hardships, with men from lower socioeconomic backgrounds suffering even harsher effects. Providing support for those in financial distress could play a vital role in preserving cognitive health in the future.

item.title: Quote of the day by LeBron James: "I think the reason why I'm the person who I am today is because…" - an inspiring lesson on resilience, adversity and the power of difficult beginnings
item.description: LeBron James credits his difficult childhood for shaping his current character and perspective. He views past hardships as the essential foundation for his achievements. These challenging experiences fostered patience, gratitude, and determination within him. His journey demonstrates that starting circumstances do not permanently define one's future. Real success often carries a responsibility to help others facing similar struggles.

item.title: 150-year-overdue library book returned in Australia; racks up Rs 16 lakh 'late fee'
item.description: A library received a book returned after 150 years overdue. The calculated late fee reached approximately twenty-eight thousand Australian dollars. This rare book was discovered during home renovations and was damaged. It was borrowed by a local resident's great-great-grandfather in the 1870s. The book will now join the library's local history collection.

item.title: California vineyards used owl boxes to attract barn owls, reducing rodent numbers by up to 52%
item.description: A new study from California has found that barn owls help vineyards control rodents naturally by both hunting them and making them more cautious. Researchers observed up to 52% fewer rodents in vineyards with more owls. The findings suggest that encouraging barn owls through nest boxes could reduce the need for pesticides while supporting biodiversity and sustainable farming.
